description: Armenian kingdom (ancient – medieval) in the South Caucasus whose conversion to Christianity (301 CE) made it the first Christian state in the world; Armenian political history alternated between Persian, Byzantine, Arab, Mongol, and Turkish overlordship while Armenian cultural identity was preserved through the unique Armenian alphabet (created 405 CE), the Apostolic Church, and a literate merchant diaspora that spread from the Mediterranean to India.

temporal.notes: Stub: dates from GeoJSON basemap years 700–1200

lifecycle_phases.description: Armenian nobility (nakharars) maintained semi-independence under alternating Byzantine and Sasanian suzerainty.
Arab conquest ended Arsacid rule; Armenians endured as subordinate marzpanate while preserving church and alphabet.
Bagratid dynasty unified Armenian principalities and established a cultural renaissance centred on Ani.
Seljuk conquest of Ani (1064) dispersed Armenians; diaspora communities formed the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia in the south.
Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia flourished as a Crusader-era maritime state until Mamluk conquest in 1375.

rise_factors.description: Armenian Apostolic Church and unique alphabet created cultural identity resistant to conquest.
Mountain terrain of the Armenian Plateau impeded full conquest by any single power.
Bagratid dynasty effectively united nakharar nobility under a single crown.

decline_factors.description: Permanent location between Byzantine, Sasanian, Arab, and Seljuk powers meant constant military pressure.
Fall of Ani in 1064 ended Armenian statehood in the homeland for centuries.
Cilician Armenia's survival depended on Crusader support that evaporated after Acre fell (1291).
